Most species are declining due to human-induced perturbations: habitat destruction
and fragmentation, climate change, pollution, over-hunting and fishing, and the
introduction of exotic species.

Stopping this biological erosion has become a major challenge for humanity.
Proactive biodiversity conservation and management imply a deep understanding of
the processes determining species and population viability. My research in
quantitative ecology is driven by this goal to protect biodiversity.

In my research group we combine observations, experiments and modelling, in the
field and in the laboratory, to study how species react to changes in their
environment. Our main model species are butterflies and protists.

## Main research interests

::: theme
::: {}
### Metapopulation dynamics

Metapopulations are groups of local populations inhabiting a fragmented landscape,
persisting in a balance of local extinctions and recolonizations by dispersal
movements.

Our research is focused on the interplay between local dynamics (demography) and
regional dynamics (dispersal and population synchrony).

*Our main butterfly study model since 1992 in Belgium is* Boloria eunomia*;
capture–mark–recapture informs on abundance and movements. Salmon also form
metapopulations, an understudied aspect of their biology.*
:::

![*Boloria eunomia*, mating](assets/img/boloria-mating.jpg){fig-alt="Boloria eunomia mating"}
:::

::: theme
::: {}
### Dispersal and movement ecology

Dispersal is a fundamental process for metapopulation dynamics, and more broadly
for ecological and evolutionary dynamics.

We are interested in the causes and consequences of dispersal, and how movement
behaviour of individuals interacts with landscape configuration in determining
effective dispersal and connectivity.

*We use* Tetrahymena thermophila*, a 50 µm long protist, in laboratory microcosms;
it actively moves using its cilia. In the field, butterflies move straighter
outside than inside their habitat.*
:::

![*Tetrahymena thermophila* movement trajectories](assets/img/tetrahymena-trajectories.jpg){fig-alt="Tetrahymena movement trajectories"}
:::

::: theme
::: {}
### Forecasting species viability

The ability to forecast how a species or (meta)population will perform in the
future is of prime importance to design and assess conservation and management
guidelines.

We use modelling approaches (such as Population Viability Analysis) to predict
their future according to environmental scenarios and conservation plans.

*Will* B. eunomia *survive the reintroduction of beaver? How many females must be
sterilized to prevent population explosion in Padangtegal Monkey Forest (Bali,
Indonesia)?*
:::

![Population Viability Analysis, a "crystal ball"](assets/img/pva-crystal-ball.png){fig-alt="PVA crystal ball"}
:::

::: theme
::: {}
### Developing methods for ecology

Research in ecology and evolution has much to gain from the generalization and
dissemination of methods developed for specific case studies.

Whether they are related to data collection and statistical analysis, modelling
approaches or building research devices, we are committed to make our developments
as general as possible, document them and provide them to the scientific community.

*A 3D printer turns a landscape configuration into a real microcosm for*
Tetrahymena*. Automatic image analysis is a powerful data collection method.
Capture–mark–recapture is a standard, reliable but costly procedure to estimate
population sizes — simpler and less costly alternatives are highly desirable for
conservation and population ecologists.*
:::

![Automatic image analysis of *Tetrahymena*](assets/img/image-analysis.png){fig-alt="Tetrahymena picture analysis"}
:::
